text:
Yes—there is such a thing as a duty to oneself, and in many cases a person can do something wrong even if they harm only themselves.

Here is one defensible position:

## Claim
A person has duties to themselves because they are not merely a tool for their own preferences; they are a being with rational agency, dignity, and a life that can go better or worse. On this view, self-harm can be morally wrong even when no one else is directly harmed.

## Why there can be duties to oneself

### 1. You can wrong your own rational agency
If you are capable of choosing, reflecting, and setting ends, then you owe it to yourself to respect that capacity. Some actions treat your future self as disposable, as if your long-term plans, commitments, and values did not matter. That can be a kind of self-betrayal.

For example, repeatedly intoxicated driving, deliberate self-starvation, or reckless addiction may not just “affect private choice.” They can express a failure to take your own agency seriously.

### 2. Some harms are wrong because they degrade the person
Not all moral wrongs require a victim distinct from the agent. If a person ruins their health, destroys their talents, or deforms their character through vice or self-abandonment, that may be wrong because it makes their life worse in a deep sense.

Even if no one else is injured, there is still a subject whose life is diminished. Morality is not only about harm to others; it also concerns what one owes to one’s own flourishing.

### 3. The absence of dependents does not remove all moral accountability
It is true that if someone has no dependents and no one else is affected, they may have a weaker case for *legal* interference or social punishment. But moral wrongness and legal enforceability are different.

A person can do something morally bad in private without deserving punishment by others. The fact that no one else is directly harmed just means the wrong is self-directed, not that it is nonexistent.

## Objection: “If it’s my life, it’s my choice”
This is the strongest challenge. One might argue that autonomy means I may use my life however I want, even foolishly. On this view, self-harm is at worst imprudent, not immoral.

### Reply
Autonomy is not the same as permission to disregard one’s own good. Freedom is valuable because it lets a person pursue a meaningful life, not because it licenses self-destruction. A choice can be voluntary and still wrong if it expresses contempt for one’s own worth or undermines one’s capacity for future choice.

## A balanced conclusion
So, if someone harms only themselves, they may still have done something wrong—though not necessarily something others should punish. The wrong lies in failing to respect their own dignity, agency, and well-being.

If you want, I can also give:
- a Kantian argument for duties to oneself,
- a utilitarian argument,
- or the strongest opposing view that there are no duties to oneself.
